sourceElements.sourceMath: Examine the original seating arrangement figure with six square tables and four spots shown around each. What do you notice or wonder? Which unknowns need decisions? Teacher reviews spoken observations.

Using 16 identical square tables and games requiring 2, 4, 5 or 10 people, state your assumptions (which games, how many simultaneous groups, occupied seats, joins and unused chairs). Teachers judge feasibility.

Design and explain an original seating plan or poster. Label all 16 available tables, their orientation, which adjacent sides are blocked by joins, and how many guests can participate in each selected game.

sourceElements.sourceActivity: Activity 2: Game Night on a Graph
sourceElements.sourceMath: Make your own scaled bar graph showing guests playing games A, B, C and D under your plan. Add a title, four labels and an interval step GREATER than 1. Justify the scale and verify agreement with the seating poster.
Compare which design assumptions changed seating capacity and explain why differently scaled graphs can communicate the same numbers.
